theme: Survival maths: why protecting the downside decides who is still trading next year

posts.topic: Drawdown recovery asymmetry: the deeper the loss, the steeper the climb back, and how risk per trade sets the depth

slides.title: A **50%** loss needs a **100%** gain to recover
slides.body: The maths that decides who's still trading next year.

slides.title: To recover from a 10% loss
To recover from a 30% loss
To recover from a 50% loss
slides.body: Half the account gone means you must **double** what's left. Formula: 1 ÷ (1 − loss) − 1.

slides.title: Same 10 losses. Very different damage.
slides.body: 10 straight losses at 1% risk: about **−9.6%**. At 5% risk: about **−40%**, which needs roughly +67% just to break even.

slides.title: Save this before your next drawdown
slides.body: Share it with the trading friend who sizes up after a loss.

posts.caption:
Losses and gains aren't symmetric. That one fact quietly ends most trading accounts.

When your account shrinks, every future % gain is calculated on a smaller base. So the deeper the hole, the steeper the climb:

−10% needs +11.1%
−30% needs +42.9%
−50% needs +100%

The formula: required gain = 1 ÷ (1 − loss) − 1.

The part most people miss: you don't control whether a losing streak arrives. You do control how deep it digs. Risk 1% per trade and 10 straight losses leaves you around −9.6%. Risk 5% and the same streak leaves you near −40%, needing roughly +67% just to get back to where you started.

Risk per trade is the one dial that decides which side of this curve you live on.

Save this, and send it to someone who's planning to "win it back."

Educational content, not financial advice.

posts.topic: Six-point pre-trade checklist that turns impulses into decisions

slides.title: 6 checks before **any** entry
items: Reason for the trade in one line
Daily loss limit not yet hit

posts.caption:
Most bad trades are decided before the entry, not after it.

A checklist won't make a trade win. What it does is make every loss a planned loss: known size, known exit, known reason. That's what keeps a drawdown shallow, which, as Monday's maths showed, is what keeps you in the game.

One extra rule that makes this work: if you can't fill in every line within about 10 seconds, that's your answer. Hesitation usually means the trade is an impulse looking for a justification.

The "reason in one line" item matters more than it looks. Later, when you review your journal, it's the only way to tell a good trade that lost from a bad trade that got lucky.

Save this and run through it before your next entry. Share it with the friend who trades straight off a notification.

posts.topic: Losing streaks are statistically normal; the reaction to them is the real danger

slides.title: **Five losses** in a row don't prove your strategy is broken.
slides.body: What a losing streak actually means, in numbers.

slides.title: A 40% win rate can still be profitable
slides.body: Illustrative: win 2R, lose 1R. Expectancy = 0.4 × 2 − 0.6 × 1 = **+0.2R** per trade.

slides.title: Chance any 5 trades all lose
slides.body: At a 40% win rate, each trade loses 60% of the time. 0.6⁵ ≈ **7.8%**, about 1 in 13.

slides.title: Over 200 trades, a 5-loss streak is near-certain
slides.body: With odds like that, streaks aren't a warning sign. They're **the cost** of running a positive-expectancy strategy.

slides.title: The streak isn't the danger. The **reaction** is.
slides.body: At 1% risk, five losses is about −4.9%. Doubling size to win it back is how a normal dip becomes an account-level event.

slides.title: Decide this **before** the streak
items: Stop after a set daily loss
Change rules in review, never mid-session

slides.title: Save this for your next red week
slides.body: Send it to the friend who just said their strategy stopped working.

posts.caption:
Five losses in a row doesn't mean your strategy stopped working. Here's the maths.

Take an illustrative strategy that wins 40% of the time at 2R and loses 60% at 1R. Expectancy is +0.2R per trade. Profitable over time.

Yet any five trades in a row will all lose about 7.8% of the time. Over a few hundred trades, that streak is close to guaranteed to show up.

The extra insight: judge your strategy on a large sample, and judge yourself on every trade. Ask "did I follow my rules?" after each loss, not "did it work?" Twenty trades can't tell you much about an edge. One trade can tell you a lot about your discipline.

Most blown accounts don't come from the streak itself. They come from what the trader did during it.

Save this for the next red week, and share it with someone in one right now.

Educational content, not financial advice.

posts.topic: High win rate does not equal profitability; expectancy depends on payoff size

slides.title: A high win rate means a **profitable** strategy.
slides.body: Win 70% at +0.5R, lose 30% at −1.5R: expectancy = 0.35 − 0.45 = **−0.1R** per trade. Win rate without payoff is half the story.

posts.caption:
A 70% win rate can lose money. Steadily.

Expectancy is what matters: (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss).

In this illustrative example, 70% of trades win 0.5R and 30% lose 1.5R. That's 0.35R − 0.45R = −0.1R per trade. Over 100 trades, roughly −10R. It feels good almost every day and still drains the account.

The extra insight: high win rates often come from habits that hide risk. Taking profit early, then widening or removing the stop on losers so they "have room to come back." The win rate climbs while the average loss quietly grows.

That's why tracking only wins and losses misleads you. Log the R of every trade, and your real numbers show up within weeks.

posts.topic: Fixed lot sizes create hidden variable risk; size from risk % and stop distance (Zenlot weekly mention)

slides.title: Same lot size every trade? Your risk isn't **fixed**.
slides.body: Why "I always trade 0.5 lots" isn't a risk plan.

slides.title: Same lots, different stops, different risk
slides.body: USD 5,000 account on EURUSD (~$10 a pip per lot). 0.5 lots with a 25-pip stop risks $125 (**2.5%**). Same lots, 60-pip stop: $300 (**6%**).

slides.title: Size from **risk**, not habit
slides.body: Lots = risk $ ÷ (stop in pips × pip value per lot). Choose risk first, place the stop second, calculate size last.

slides.title: 1% risk, 25-pip stop, USD 5,000 account
slides.body: $50 risk ÷ (25 pips × $10) = **0.2 lots**. If the stop is hit, you lose about $50.

slides.title: Set your risk **once**
slides.body: Example account: CAD 2,064 at **2%** risk. Zenlot recommends a lot size for every trade.

slides.title: Save this formula for your next trade
slides.body: Prefer not to do it by hand every time? Try **Zenlot**, link in bio.

posts.caption:
Trading the same lot size every time feels consistent. It isn't.

Your risk is lot size × stop distance × pip value. Keep the lots fixed and your risk swings with every stop you place. On a USD 5,000 account trading EURUSD, 0.5 lots can mean 2.5% risk on one trade and 6% on the next.

The fix is to reverse the order: decide the risk, place the stop where the trade is invalid, then calculate the size.

The extra insight: fixed-% sizing also protects you in drawdowns. As the account shrinks, 1% becomes a smaller dollar amount, so your position size shrinks automatically. That slows the slide, which, as Monday's maths showed, makes recovery far easier.

Pip values vary by pair and account currency, so check yours. Or let Zenlot calculate it before every entry. Link in bio.
